chunks: "In most cases you don't change a target's address in software; you choose it in hardware, and if that isn't possible you work around it. I'd go through the options in order.
Many parts have one to three pins, such as ADDR or A0 to A2, that you tie to ground or supply, and sometimes SDA or SCL, to pick among two to eight addresses.
An ADS1115-style ADC, for example, gets four addresses depending on where its ADDR pin goes.
Second, some devices let you program a new address through a register, like many time-of-flight sensors.
Those usually come up at a default address with all copies identical, so you hold all but one in shutdown with their enable pins, change the one's address, release the next, and so on.
The register is often volatile, so you redo it after every power cycle.
Third, if you can't change addresses, you isolate the devices: an I2C multiplexer like the TCA9548 amps gives each device its own branch, or you put them on a second I2C bus.
Finally, there's dynamic addressing in SMBus and I3C, where the host assigns addresses.
And before any of this, I make sure it isn't just the 7-bit versus 8-bit confusion, like 0x90 versus 0x48."
